claims.claim: Evagrius was ordained as a reader by Basil of Caesarea and later served as a deacon and archdeacon under Gregory of Nazianzus in Constantinople, where he participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.

Evagrius left Constantinople around 382, joined a monastic community in Jerusalem led by Rufinus and Melania the Elder, took monastic vows in 383, and then spent the rest of his life in the Egyptian desert at Nitria and Kellia.
De malignis cogitationibus (Greek title: Περὶ διαφορῶν πονηρῶν λογισμῶν, 'On Various Evil Thoughts') is a relatively lengthy treatise of 43 sections.

In De malignis cogitationibus, Evagrius analyzes closely the tactics of demons and the counterattacks available to the ascetic, explains relationships between the various evil thoughts, and provides a glimpse into the epistemic, anthropological, and cosmological notions that undergird his advice on spiritual warfare.
Only the first half (about twenty-three chapters) of De malignis cogitationibus was reproduced in the Philokalia published by Nikodemos the Hagiorite.
The Greek text survives in the Patrologia Graeca and has been critically edited by Géhin, Guillaumont, and Guillaumont in Sources chrétiennes 438 (Paris: Éditions du Cerf, 1998).
The work was transmitted under the name of Nilus of Ancyra (sub nomine Nili Ancyrani) in some manuscript traditions.

Evagrius developed the first major philosophical-theological exposition of monastic mysticism by developing the Neoplatonic biblical theology of Origen, and his teachings laid the groundwork for a tradition of spiritual life in both Eastern and Western churches.
Evagrius was a teacher of John Cassian and Palladius of Galatia, and his works were translated into Syriac and Armenian, influencing Syrian as well as Byzantine spirituality.

Within some strands of late ancient Christianity, Evagrius's teachings were no longer considered orthodox later in his life or after his death, although the Armenian and Syrian churches continued to cherish his writings.
